blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A crew-hiring MILP minimizes cost. Its LP relaxation's optimal value is 8,200. A planner proposes a plan that keeps every rule and costs 8,050. What should the analyst conclude?

options.text: The plan is a new optimum, since it beats the LP relaxation's value
options.says: When minimizing, the LP value is a floor: no allowed plan can cost less than 8,200.

options.text: The plan is allowed but not optimal, since the LP value is a ceiling
options.says: When minimizing the LP value is a floor, not a ceiling, and 8,050 sits below it.

options.text: The plan's figure must be wrong, since the LP value is a floor
options.says: Right: every allowed plan is a point of the relaxation, so none can cost less than its optimum.

options.text: The plan is an outlier, since the LP value is an average of plans
options.says: The LP value is the best point of the relaxation, not an average; it bounds every plan.

origin.section: Every Allowed Plan Is a Point of the Relaxation, So the LP Value Bounds Every Plan

questions.stem: A maximizing selection model has LP bound 5,250 and best plan 5,000. A colleague's rounded plan is worth 4,800. What is the integrality gap?

options.text: 5%, from the bound's distance above the best plan's value
options.says: Right: (5,250 - 5,000) / 5,000 = 5%; the rounded plan plays no part in it.

options.text: 9.4%, from the bound's distance above the rounded plan's value
options.says: The gap compares the bound with the best plan, not with some other plan.

options.text: 4.8%, from the bound's distance as a share of the bound's value
options.says: The gap is a share of the best plan's value, not of the bound.

options.text: 4%, from the best plan's distance above the rounded plan's value
options.says: That measures the rounded plan's shortfall, which is not the integrality gap.

origin.section: The Integrality Gap Is the Distance From the LP Bound to the Best Plan

questions.stem: Two modelers write "build the substation only if the feeder is built" as x_s <= x_f and as x_s <= 5 x_f. Both models are solved to optimality on the same data. What differs?

options.text: The optimum, since the second row allows more 0/1 plans
options.says: With binaries both rows allow exactly the same plans, so the optimum is the same.

options.text: Nothing, since the two rows allow the same 0/1 plans
options.says: Same 0/1 plans, but not the same fractional points: the LP relaxations differ.

options.text: The plan, since the second row lets the substation go first
options.says: With x_f = 0 the row reads x_s <= 0, so the substation still needs the feeder.

options.text: The LP bound, since the second row allows more fractional points
options.says: Right: x_f = 0.2 already allows x_s = 1, so the relaxation can reach higher and the gap can grow.

origin.section: Two Correct Formulations Can Have Different Gaps
